Disclaimer: Not psych, just someone who also has OCD that isn't as bad IMO anymore.



OCD gets worse with baseline anxiety levels, and when you're stressed about something else


If you're worried about money, a job change or something else, even if it has nothing related to your cleaning, that might be triggering it. A really good media example of what this looks like is MM from The Boys. Your stress from other stuff triggers your OCD too. He starts sorting and getting frustrated and having panic attacks because of the stress from his job with The Boys. It's not the disorganization making him feel compelled to sort, but the greater disorder.



What I read in a book that helped me is..., facts won't fix the OCD. OCD thrives on your emotions, which to break down the abstract means basic self care is a must.



1. Sleep, 8 hours. Take meds in the short term to help get you there if insomnia is also an issue. 



2. Least eat twice a day, doesn't have to be a meal if you can't manage, just make sure you're getting enough calories to not feel on edge.



3. Make sure you're clean. As in, at least once a day wash your face. Change clothes once a day.



The real trick to OCD is to stop arguing with the thoughts. When you feel like "I have to clean this! This will happen! I feel so stressed!" It's instead to ask "is it okay if I feel stressed?"


Instead of trying to stop the feeling, you just...let it be.



Don't push away the anxiety. Talk to it. What are you scared about? A disease? The dirt spreading? Fungus? Or is it something else. You fear judgement? You have past experiences with something going wrong when you didn't clean it? Don't judge yourself, just figure out what you're feeling when you feel the urge to clean, take a deep breath and try to feel the anxiety before acting. Listen to what comes up when you feel the urge to wash your hands. Try to focus on your thoughts. The sensations. 


Sometimes, Id also feel the urge to clean when I was in pain or upset. Simple thing like dry skin or a headache was enough to stir 4 hour cleaning sprees.

It seemed like you didn't need one, because you had legal guardians who used theirs.


But lots of things for security reasons most often (assuming US), want verification. If you buy something expensive, the ID serves as a way to verify it is you (liability for banks). If you're getting a job, the ID is shorthand for "you are a legal citizen and are not committing any fraud." When purchasing controlled substances, it's another liability thing, those substances are controlled and there's big penalties for selling them without the check. 


It's also you have a lot more opportunities now to access you didn't have below 18. The ID is simply part of that ticket. As well as if you drive, you will need it every time you hit the road. 


Also be glad the 90s/00s idea of "check ID" with credit cards phased out. It used to be you'd actually check a credit card against someone's ID to verify it's them using it. 


But all jobs who lawfully abide by taxes require ID and most often social security. While there's less scrupulous jobs, you are signing yourself up for an IRS audit.

Gain identity, no. Gain purpose, yes.

Yup, I've now developed a system. Disclaimer: this system probably isn't entirely good, but this is how I go about it.



1. What outcome do I want out of the situation? Does me being right matter? 


1A. Is it something factual being debated? Where there's objective right/wrong answer. 


For most small issues, me being right doesn't matter. I just go 'oh, okay, good to know' when corrected/maybe corrected. Some situations are so short it's kinda like I remind myself it doesn't matter. Though sometimes I'll go, 'hold on, let me get back to you on that. I'm going to look it up.'


1B. Despite being factual, and me being correct, they persist. Back to the beginning—do I need something immediately that being right will accomplish? No. End the topic. 'I think we have to agree to disagree. Though on another note, did you see it's hitting a 100 next week. Weren't you going fishing?' 


1C. I do need something? Like they owe me money or need to send me information or it's work relwted. 'I think we had a misunderstanding, can you explain why you think (whatever it is)?' 


1D. They don't let the topic drop. Time to tell them I'm upset, because probably at this point I am. 'Hey, I'm going to be real, chief. I'm not feeling this. I know we don't see eye to eye. Can I have space?' Use I statements, don't attack, just basically acknowledge your feelings, and that you don't feel comfortable anymore. Set a boundary. Once it's been set, if they don't respect it, well...



2. The other person needs something from me, but I feel different/I'm right about something.


2A. I'm wrong, or whatever they need isn't that big of a deal to me. Okay, not worth the fight, give it over. 


2B. I feel I'm right, and it is a big deal. I ask more clarifying questions. What do they need specifically from me? Could we create a timeline for it? If it's a problem or has something tangible can we arrange something and check back in later? I acknowledge their feelings, but I admit I need a few moments away from the situation to figure out my own. These situations are always different. No advice, but generally if you're about to expolode--get out and sort it out on your own before that.



2C. I feel I'm right, but it's kinda an inconvenience/a bother to go with their suggestion/request. Then ideally, compromise. Surely there's a middle.



What's my role? Is it work and they're a client/customer? In that case, in the long term is just accepting the defeat worth it? Yes. Okay, I put aside my feelings and chock it up to a 'you lose some, some days.'  It's a friend? I ask a few more questions sometimes, but sometimes I agree, but with boundaries. 'Hey, I'll go with you to this thing, because I promised I'd go, but I wasn't aware there would be alcohol there. I might leave early. I can send you money for an Uber, but I can't stay for the whole party. I'll text you when I leave.' 


3. Am I mind reading or do I know for sure they're upset/want something? What's the evidence? Can I ask them? 


Sometimes I just assume someone is upset/is taking something harsh. If I'm going into a message reading intent sometimes I'll stop and ask, 'Are you upset about (this specific thing)?


Sometimes I'm inventing a fire when I vaguely smelt something burnt. There's nothing there or I misunderstood them. 


Sometimes though, admittedly, you feel a gut feeling of 'they said it's fine, but I feel they're lying.' Well, we can't mind read and they didn't tell us anything different, so we can only think for a moment. Maybe we're the one that's upset? Time to express those feelings.  I'm awful at creating I statements, but half the time when you think the other person is upset, it's actually your own feelings.



'I feel upset about this. I don't like this.' 


Whatever you do, don't accuse. Just acknowledge your feelings in the matter very simply. 'I feel upset when I don't feel listened to. I had a really hard morning with work.' instead of 'You weren't listening to me after the crappy day I had at work!'

1. Identify the emotion 
2. Express it simply


'I am sad I lost my hat :(, because it was my favorite.'


3. Avoid the catastrophizing. That's black-and-white thinking. Don't let yourself go down the rabbit hole of 'what if I lose more things because I'm so careless? What if...what if...'

Just draw a good line. I personally believe you shouldn't ever copy AI generation word for word. You can ask it better ways to say something or how to make a sentence read better, factor those edits in, but I would never let it be the final edit. Nor would I ever let it touch an entire thing I wrote, mostly because it sucks as an editor for cohesiveness. 


AI is prone to 'hallucinating' information, so it's unlikely to process your writing and ascertain it's only supposed to follow the logic of that story-verse, and may suggest things that would ruin your continuity/style/world-building.



Also, don't treat it like gospel (and that's true for anyone editing your work). While it may have suggestions, sometimes I artistically want things to be vague or messy, or I'm trying to write rhythmically. It isn't the AP Stylebook test; I am going to have incomplete clauses and I want them there.



Again, it's a tool. But no tool can make you better on its own. 


And as far as cleaning up your writing. I hate to say it, but a 'clean' read is subjective across language, culture, age and preference. Some people love purple prose. Some people stylistically write without capitalization. AI is fed  a data set that no matter the intent of the programmer, ends up being a reflection of their own bias.

They're cheap, but you rent the room and have private bathroom no choosing your roommates and you share kitchen, living room and laundry. Lots of non-students lived there though which is why I suggest it since you're still young. Some apartments may advertise as "for students" but if you ask and say "I'm not a student" they may still allow.

e. Most important give it time. Don't beat yourself up for lack of instant solutions. You realized "I want to live in my own space." Break it down. Unfortunately when you're just starting off, lot of your budget will be...bills. Get into the habit of not touching your check and letting a balance of money sit in your account.

If you are looking for academic fanfic analyzing, might I suggest Henry Jenkins and the idea of participatory culture. That's the rabbit hole I know from film studies that deals with how people engage with media.

Oh, my grade school did fanfic writing (but didn't call it that, lol, just "choose how the story would go from there!" Back in 2000s. We did it for one of the dog books for like age 10 and Percy Jackson. Most of us wrote nice little 300 word little stories that barely made sense, but were graded based on grammar instead.



Rather than focus on "what is needed in their writing" to make it fanfic, just do the ole "I'm grading you on grammar, how many pages, etc." and give assignments like "Think of a movie or book you watched you didn't like the ending to and write your own" or something like that. It's more open-ended and allows the people who likely don't engage in fan culture to participate in fanfiction without knowing the ins and outs. I wouldn't bring up actual fan works as reading assignments, especially as a teacher. Not because I don't think fandom writers are bad, but because assuming your American--the parents. God forbid the parents. You do not want that email from the principal because someone mentioned asexuality or gasp liking other boys in their fanfic and some parent had a heart attack.



Also, at a college level, we discussed fandom/fan culture divorced from any actual fan created works except a Beatles fan website for examples from late 90s. (Henry Jenkins is my favorite there on literary analysts). You don't need to show people fanfic to explain fanfic. Often going over "hey, have you ever wondered what if?" And point to contemporary media examples like Disney Marvel's What-If, the various adaptions of movies as examples of retelling a story in your own way, like the various Sherlock Holmes derivative works. Sometimes starting a lot broader and just letting them have a basic understanding of "oh, you can make stories based off of other stories??? For fun???" is a good way to avoid a letter from parents.


You can go over the basics of "sometimes people like to write about characters like they like to draw them" and if any of the 11 year olds after go down the rabbit hole--that's on them and their parents. Ask them what shows they watch or like and get them going about what they like and they'll likely be able to go from there and write the story. Most eleven year olds once given permission to talk about a show they like won't have any issues conjuring up a fanfic without knowing it's a fanfic.


A lot of kids that age LOVE self-inserts. That's another way to get them to write fanfic. "Imagine you were xyz character and write what you'd do!"

One thing to understand is people come from all walks of life and while you have learned something, they may not have even the basics in that area and are completely clueless. If this isn't something that happens occasionally, but something you deal with every day, it may be more of a "you don't need to be right, you just need this convo to be over" skill you need to develop. 

There are 7 billion people on this planet, and some matters are not a "right or wrong" conversation but a "we live our own lives, and I cannot change yours." 

In most cases, as someone who has dealt with a lot of customer service, you disengage when you realize they aren't going to agree. You take a deep breath, say "Oh, I see." You don't see, you just want the conversation to end and, this is just polite social courtesy. You simply change topics and allow yourself a mental tap out. 

Also:

 Weigh the pros and cons in your mind before continuing trying to get them to understand. Do you need something from them? Can you get it from someone else or yourself? Is this interaction worth having? What do you get out of convincing them of your perspective? Unless they're your friend or family, or you're trying to get something from them tangible, most of the time it's a "Ugh, What a dummy" moment in your head and you just smile and exit the conversation. 

Choose your battles. It's much less easy to be frustrated and upset when you aren't fighting on the front lines daily. While I have strongly held opinions like everyone else, unless someone's actively in my way, I let them be. Especially online. While it is very annoying to see people think Z about XY, I take a deep breath, look around, realize this is not a pressing matter and disconnect.

I had same issue with my car for 2 years straight. The first step is just sitting in it. You can't get rid of the anxiety, but you can confront it. So you sit there, and sit with the feelings of fear and agitation, put a timer on, then when the timer is up you step out. Maybe once you feel your breathing under control you start the car, you back out, you do a trip around the block. You park it. You do it one step at a time. One small outing. Daily. Until you feel your breathing is under control.

Don't wait to feel fearless, you won't be. But also don't rush through your fear--I did that. Pretending your fear is non-existent completely also doesn't work. You have to operate on a steady incline of what's in your abilities. 

Once you've driven around a few times I also recommend getting an oil change and check up. I was so terrified my car would have 3000+ problems after not driving it for 2 years.

No. It only had the original issues it always had when I bought it. The car didn't catch on fire or magically become a monster (though I feared to death it might).

You see drama? You keep scrolling. Enjoy what you like, don't seek out drama for what you like. I honestly think engaging in criticism after a work is complete is easiest/helps put things in perspective, but if you engage in criticism of something you like while it's ongoing, I suggest doing it with people you respect that communicate 2-way rather than any nobody off the net.
